quiz.question: What has happened to global extreme poverty since 1990?
options: It has stayed about the same

headline: You Are Statistically More Likely to Guess This at Random Than to Actually Know It
teaser: Here is a question about global poverty that has been asked to thousands of people across dozens of countries -- university professors, business leaders, journalists, Nobel laureates. The results are, by any reasonable standard, hilarious. Not only do most people get it wrong, they get it wrong so consistently and so confidently that a chimpanzee throwing darts at the answer options would outperform them. Something has happened to extreme poverty over the past thirty-five years. The question is what. And the answer, when it comes, tends to produce a silence that is worth savouring -- the particular quiet of a worldview rearranging itself in real time.
metaDescription: 74% of people believe global poverty is getting worse. It has nearly halved since 1990. Here is what actually happened, and why almost nobody noticed.
summary: A majority of people believe global extreme poverty is getting worse. They are wrong — not approximately wrong, but wrong in the specific direction of opposite. The rate has fallen from 36% of humanity in 1990 to around 10% today, representing the largest reduction in human deprivation in recorded history. It happened quietly, and most people missed it entirely.
nuance: Progress has been uneven. Sub-Saharan Africa has seen the number of people in extreme poverty rise, not fall. And the poverty line itself was revised upward in 2025, changing the count without changing underlying reality.
brysonAside: On any average day over the past thirty-five years, approximately a hundred and fifteen thousand people left extreme poverty behind. Every day. For thirty-five years.

emailDigestLine: The world's largest reduction in human deprivation in recorded history happened so quietly that most people believe the opposite occurred.
premiumTeaser: What the headline figure doesn't tell you is where this progress didn't happen — and why that matters more than the global average suggests. And then there is the question of how the measurement was built in the first place, which turns out to involve a development economist, a surprising methodology, and one of the more quietly remarkable data-assembly efforts of the twentieth century.
b2bClassroomNote: Classroom discussion: Ask students to guess the answer before showing data. Connects to SDG 1 (No Poverty) and the gap between media representation and statistical reality. Pairs with Gapminder's Dollar Street for visual context.
publishingNote: Both sources agree within 2%. Gamma nuance substantive and well-sourced. Strong shareability.

learn.title: Gapminder Dollar Street
learn.description: Dollar Street shows photographs of everyday objects — toothbrushes, stoves, front doors — sorted by income level across dozens of countries. It makes the poverty line tangible in a way that a percentage never can.

fund.description: GiveDirectly sends cash transfers to extremely poor households with no strings attached — the kind of direct intervention that moves people across the poverty line this chart tracks.
fund.impact: $30 = one month cash transfer to one household
